meta.title: JARVIS — Homelab AI Cluster
meta.description: JARVIS — a private 18-node Kubernetes homelab in production: GitOps infrastructure, fully local AI inference, a fact-grounded voice assistant and a zero-trust network.

hero.badge: PRIVATE HOMELAB PROJECT · v5.5 IN PRODUCTION
hero.description: A 18-node Kubernetes homelab that thinks and listens at home — fully declarative, with purely local AI inference, a fact-grounded voice assistant and a zero-trust network.

goLive.description: Go-live reached: all nodes joined, GPU tier accepted, voice assistant in daily use. The counter shows the time since go-live.

systemMap.title: The Entire Toolchain at a Glance
systemMap.description: JARVIS as the hub of six domains — from GitOps and local AI inference to security, voice and observability.

features.title: What JARVIS Does
features.description: From bare-metal node to speaking assistant — every capability runs on its own network, declaratively managed and versioned.

items.title: GitOps infrastructure
items.description: One Git monorepo as the single source of truth. Numbered, idempotent bootstrap scripts for the node layer, FluxCD for cluster state — every change a reviewable commit, every drift reconciled automatically.

items.title: 18-node bare-metal cluster
items.description: 14 Raspberry Pi 5, one Raspberry Pi 4, an ODROID-H5 and a GPU workstation joined as a K3s cluster with a highly available control plane — all self-hosted, no cloud VMs. Plus a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W as a watchdog outside Kubernetes.

items.title: Fully local AI inference
items.description: Requests run across tiered hardware — from Hailo NPUs on the Pis and a CPU reserve up to an RTX 5060 Ti workstation. No model call ever leaves the house. If the GPU is asleep, a fallback mode with smaller models takes over automatically.

items.title: Vision tracker (partly live)
items.description: Presence detection is already running: a camera with a local NPU reports only “someone there / nobody there”, and no image is stored. Next, the camera will follow the person with pan, tilt and zoom — still fully local.

items.title: Fact-grounded voice assistant & HUD
items.description: “Hey Jarvis”: on-device wake word, speech recognition and language model on the GPU, a British voice. The first sentence is spoken after about one second on average. Knowledge questions are answered only from cited sources — 21 offline reference works and news — with an automatic cross-check, and follow-up questions are understood in context. A holographic HUD shows search results, weather, media and system status.

items.title: Zero-trust network segmentation
items.description: Default-deny network policies per workload, WireGuard-encrypted node-to-node traffic in strict mode, a dedicated DNS filter and an explicit, versioned allow set instead of implicit reachability.

items.title: Security & compliance
items.description: Controls modelled on ISO 27001, NIS-2 and CIS: secrets only ever encrypted, signed and digest-pinned images, kernel-level runtime monitoring and automatic image scanning.

items.title: Automated version governance
items.description: Dependencies are checked continuously and proposed as reviewable pull requests — with a grace period for new releases, no silent “latest”.

items.title: Backup, DR & observability
items.description: Daily cluster backups and etcd snapshots to self-hosted S3 storage, tested restore paths, end-to-end monitoring and alerting across nodes, workloads, GPU and network. An external watchdog also checks the cluster from outside, and every Monday a weekly report sums up backups, alerts, security and energy.

items.title: Home automation & media
items.description: Home Assistant controls heating and devices by voice, knows the local weather and plays music and films from the NAS on the display, TV or speakers.

pipeline.title: Fully Declarative Rollout
pipeline.description: Every layer of the cluster is managed by a dedicated tool; every change is a commit.

modelTiers.title: The Right Hardware for Every Request
modelTiers.description: Requests are routed across tiers — from edge accelerators to the GPU workstation. There is no cloud AI.

rows.role: Last-resort tier (Qwen3 1.7B) and small models up to 4 B parameters
Fallback mode (Qwen3 4B, Qwen3.5 2B), code completion and embeddings for search
Voice and agents (gpt-oss 20B, 64k context), reasoning (Qwen3.6 35B), coding (Devstral Small 2, Qwen2.5-Coder) and images (FLUX.1, SDXL)
Whisper large-v3-turbo for speech recognition, Kokoro for speech output (Piper as reserve)
21 offline reference works, a learning knowledge store and a meta search across three sources
None: no model call leaves the house

security.title: Aligned with ISO 27001, NIS-2, and CIS
security.description: Even as a private project, run like a production system — with documented controls instead of trust by word of mouth.
highlights: Encryption of sensitive cluster data at rest
Full API audit logging with RBAC traceability
Secrets stored encrypted only in the repository (never in plaintext)
Policy enforcement, runtime threat detection, and image scanning

In-kernel runtime enforcement (Tetragon): unauthorized process starts and connections by the AI services are killed instantly — on the Raspberry Pi nodes too, thanks to a purpose-built kernel compiled from signature-verified sources
Outbound telemetry switched off for all services — no error or usage reports leave the network
Own container images are signed (cosign) and admitted only with a valid signature
Compromised upstream components are blocked and replaced — the AI gateway was swapped out entirely after a supply-chain incident
CI runs in hardened, isolated runners with no third-party actions; AI agents may only open pull requests, never run commands directly
Agents run isolated in a gVisor sandbox, with no service-account token and no host access
All Raspberry Pi cluster nodes are wired-only — Wi-Fi is disabled at the firmware level
Regular restore tests verify that the backups are actually restorable
security.footerNote: Infrastructure details, internal network addresses, and operational scripts stay private and are deliberately not published on this site.

items.title: The path of a voice request
items.body: The wake word “Hey Jarvis” is detected right on the voice terminal. The recording goes to Whisper on the GPU (under half a second); then Home Assistant decides: simple commands such as lights, heating, time or weather are handled instantly without a language model. Everything else goes to the local language model, which can use tools — web search, Wikipedia, weather, media, routes. Kokoro speaks the answer sentence by sentence: the first sentence plays while the rest is still being synthesised. On average the first sentence can be heard after about one second.

items.title: Grounded facts instead of hallucination
items.body: For knowledge and news questions Jarvis does not answer from memory. It looks things up first — in 21 offline reference works from the German Wikipedia to technical documentation, in its own knowledge store or via a self-hosted meta search — and phrases the answer only from those sources. Numbers, dates and names are checked against the source; hard, multi-step questions are planned in a dedicated research loop. If there is no evidence, Jarvis says so honestly. Whatever it lacked is researched daily by a learning service — only sourced facts are kept.

items.title: Home automation & n8n
items.body: Home Assistant brings together radiator thermostats, TV, speakers and weather data. Jarvis greets you on arrival with the weather and a rain preview and plays media from the NAS on the right device. n8n is ready for further automations; workflows are versioned in the same Git repository as the infrastructure.

items.title: The Kubernetes cluster (K3s)
items.body: K3s is a lean Kubernetes distribution for edge and ARM hardware. Three nodes form the highly available control plane with etcd, the rest work as workers. FluxCD continuously reconciles the cluster with the Git repository — manual changes are reverted automatically. Longhorn replicates storage across the nodes, Cilium encrypts all traffic between them with WireGuard. The complete state is reproducible from a single repository.

power.title: Estimated Power Consumption
power.description: Realistic estimate per device in typical operation (idle to light load) as an indication of the order of magnitude — now complemented by real power measurement in the cluster.

rows.label: GPU workstation HP Z840 + RTX 5060 Ti (always on, idle)

power.wolBody: The GPU workstation (HP Z840) has the largest single draw in the cluster at over 300 W peak. It now switches itself off at night once nobody is in the room and the GPU is idle, and wakes via Wake-on-LAN — on presence or by voice. Until it is ready, JARVIS answers in fallback mode.
power.upsBody: An APC Back-UPS Pro 900 rides out brief outages and voltage dips. Its own continuous draw — inverter standby plus trickle charging — is around 5 W. Next, it will shut the nodes down automatically and cleanly during longer outages.

savings.label: Let the GPU workstation sleep at night and in quiet phases via Wake-on-LAN
Spin down the backup drive between backup runs
Switch the HUD display off automatically when nobody is home

power.measuredBody: The cluster measures its own consumption: the 7-day average is about 121 W (range 84–367 W), roughly €25 a month at 28 ct/kWh. Without the GPU server it is about 105 W, and a Pi 5 needs 3–6 W — the night shutdown works.

items.title: Fallback mode without the GPU server
items.desc: If the GPU server is off, smaller reserve models keep answering — on the CPU reserve and, as the last resort, permanently loaded on the edge NPU. Stop, playback and jokes need no model at all. In fallback mode, places, routes and weather are answered by fixed functions instead of letting the small model guess.

items.title: Answers without a language model
items.desc: Percentages, roots, conversions, time, days until holidays, calendar week as well as pods, nodes and alerts are computed or queried exactly — in under 0.1 seconds.

items.title: Always metric, units spoken out
items.desc: Miles, feet, pounds and Fahrenheit from sources are converted automatically; “km/h” or “°C” are spoken out instead of spelled.

items.title: 7-day weather
items.desc: With weekday plus “today” and “tomorrow” — weekend questions can be answered too.

items.title: “Is it open now?”
items.desc: Opening hours from map data are evaluated, even past midnight; if one map service fails, a second takes over at once.

items.title: Distances and routes
items.desc: “Is Rome or Paris closer to Zurich?” is recognised and calculated; places like “main station” are resolved correctly.

items.title: Explanation questions
items.desc: For “How does … work?” JARVIS looks specifically for the working principle.

items.title: Follow-up questions
items.desc: “Who was Einstein?” – “Where did he die?” JARVIS resolves references like “he” or “that city” from the conversation before looking things up.

items.title: Research loop for hard questions
items.desc: For multi-step questions, comparisons or explanations JARVIS plans what to look up and checks the result — in 2 to 4 seconds. For example: which river flows through Mozart’s birthplace?

items.title: Exact arithmetic
items.desc: Calculations and unit conversions are computed exactly instead of estimated.

items.title: Memory
items.desc: “Remember that …”, “forget …”, “what do you know about me?” — remembered facts feed into relevant answers, even in fallback mode.

items.title: Stricter fact grounding
items.desc: Numbers, dates and names must appear in the sources, years exactly. Without evidence JARVIS honestly says it has no reliable source — made-up people stay made up. Numbers are given as digits so the check reliably catches them.

items.title: Mute mode
items.desc: “Be quiet” or “mute for 30 minutes”: JARVIS stays silent, announcements are held back, then it resumes on its own.

items.title: Status report by voice
items.desc: Cluster, power, drive temperatures and open security findings on request.

groups.title: Knowledge & learning

items.title: 21 offline reference works
items.desc: Besides the German Wikipedia: a dictionary, travel guides, quotations, textbooks, repair guides, Linux and developer documentation and Q&A archives. JARVIS picks the right one itself.

items.title: Faster lookups
items.desc: New topics in 0.12 s on average instead of up to 2 s; infobox facts such as area, population or elevation are read too.

items.title: Learning loop without manual training
items.desc: When a source is missing or the user corrects JARVIS, a learning service researches the case thoroughly every day. Only sourced answers with verified numbers enter the knowledge store — corrections are checked, not taken on trust.

items.title: Nothing forgotten
items.desc: Everything learned is re-checked by the nightly quality test; the weekly report shows issues, learnings and open items.

items.title: Search engine mix
items.desc: Our own meta search now queries three sources instead of one — median response 0.64 instead of up to 4 seconds.

groups.note: Deliberately no weight training: fine-tuning teaches style, not reliable facts, and can push out what was learned. Sourced, retrievable knowledge is safer — data for a later fine-tune is still being collected.

items.title: Hermes Agent
items.desc: Research assistant in the messenger with web search via our own meta search, memory and a task list — deliberately without file access or shell.

items.title: ZeroClaw
items.desc: Second agent in an isolated sandbox: no internet, no shell, only its own working folder.

items.title: A mailbox of its own for the agent
items.desc: A small broker service gives ZeroClaw access to exactly one mailbox. Sending, forwarding and deleting only after confirmation, recipients fixed.

items.title: Real tool list
items.desc: Agents receive a structured tool list instead of a text description — no more empty answers; risky tools were removed.

items.title: n8n with local AI
items.desc: Automations connected to the local models, account with two-factor sign-in.

items.title: Better mail delivery
items.desc: A 30-day test is to show how outgoing mail arrives more reliably.

items.title: Model comparison with numbers
items.desc: Newer models (Qwen3.8 27B, Gemma 4 26B, Qwen3.6 35B) were tested against the running gpt-oss 20B. Result: the current model stays — fastest and with the most passed questions.

items.title: Quality test with 110 questions
items.desc: Every night 110 questions in eight categories — from knowledge and hard questions to fallback mode and learned facts; most recently 110 of 110 with a median of 1.5 seconds.

items.title: Model comparison (Promptfoo)
items.desc: Weekly automatic comparison of all models on German test questions.

items.title: LLM tracing (Langfuse)
items.desc: Every AI request with response time and token usage — so improvements become measurable.

items.title: AI lab (JupyterLab, MLflow, Unsloth)
items.desc: GPU experimentation environment with fine-tuning; a housekeeping service clears caches and reports unused items in the weekly report instead of deleting them.

items.title: Image generation in the chat (ComfyUI)
items.desc: FLUX.1 creates images right in the chat interface, plus SDXL — fully local. Language and image model share the GPU automatically.

items.title: Document conversion (Docling)
items.desc: PDFs, Office files and images, tables included, become structured text — now also directly in the chat for uploaded files.

items.title: Annotation (Label Studio)
items.desc: Label our own images and texts for training.

items.title: Camera analysis (Frigate)
items.desc: Detects people and animals and stores only events — fully local, home network only.

items.title: Coding consistency test
items.desc: 16 programming tasks × 3 runs, code executed offline — four local models each scored 48 of 48.

items.title: Weekly model check
items.desc: A lab job checks every week that all models load and solve tasks correctly; failures raise an alert.

items.title: Larger context for agents
items.desc: The main model works with a 64,000-token context and two parallel requests.

items.title: Night shutdown of the GPU server
items.desc: Switches off once nobody is in the room and the GPU is idle; wakes when someone enters or by voice, with fallback mode bridging the start-up.

items.title: Real power measurement
items.desc: Consumption per device measured instead of estimated, with total kWh and cost in dashboards and on the kiosk HUD.

items.title: Drive health
items.desc: Temperature, wear and throttling of every SSD and NVMe every minute, with thresholds and alerts.

items.title: Weekly report
items.desc: Every Monday: backups, alerts, security, energy, drives — now also with “AI lab” and “Learning” sections.

items.title: External watchdog with dead man’s switch
items.desc: A separate mini computer checks the cluster from outside and raises the alarm if even monitoring fails.

items.title: Automatic patching
items.desc: All nodes are updated and rebooted one after another — without downtime.

items.title: Backups for the GPU server too
items.desc: The GPU server’s local data is backed up automatically whenever it is running.

items.title: Second backup on a separate drive
items.desc: All backups and the GPU server’s local data are additionally mirrored to a dedicated drive and verified by checksum; a test restore succeeded.

items.title: Tidier operations
items.desc: Finished jobs disappear after three days, and backup maintenance keeps only the latest run.

items.title: “Services” dashboard
items.desc: Mail, camera and AI requests at a glance.

items.title: Automated maintenance
items.desc: A weekly job checks for new versions of the reference works — with checksum and a 14-day waiting period — and flags due maintenance steps; results appear in the weekly report.

items.title: More cluster storage
items.desc: A previously unused drive now serves as cluster storage; the reference works live there locally.

items.title: Network switch in monitoring
items.desc: Link, traffic and errors per port in a dedicated dashboard and as a tile on the HUD; alerts for a disconnected node or a faulty cable.

items.title: HUD in the “Nachtblau” design
items.desc: Glass panels in blue, cyan and violet, a neural network at the core, no scan lines — the model for this website’s design.

items.title: Quieter at idle
items.desc: The LLM-tracing database now needs a tenth of the CPU time at idle; the energy dashboard shows the GPU server’s state instantly.

items.title: Own kernel for all Pis
items.desc: Self-built with deeper security monitoring and fixes for the network driver — first on a test Pi, then on all Pis, with rollback.

items.title: Updates with a backup first
items.desc: Storage, backup, camera and Git server updated, plus packages on all Pis; a backup before every update, and a test restore succeeded.

items.title: More reliable update automation
items.desc: Dependencies are checked without rate limits, checksums fully added.

items.title: New alerts
items.desc: For unusable models, pods evicted for lack of memory and more precise ones for the database backup.

items.title: Vulnerability watch
items.desc: Checks every service against known vulnerabilities several times a day, with dedicated alerts for mail, camera and storage.

items.title: Single sign-on with two factors
items.desc: Documents, photos and LLM tracing are only reachable through the central sign-in with a second factor.

items.title: Password manager (Vaultwarden)
items.desc: Our own Bitwarden-compatible password manager; all credentials are stored in it, encrypted.

items.title: Own mail server + webmail
items.desc: E-mail on our own domain with spam filtering and DKIM/SPF/DMARC, now with several mailboxes.

items.title: Second alert channel (ntfy)
items.desc: Push notifications to the phone in addition to the existing messenger channel.

items.title: Document management (Paperless-ngx)
items.desc: Scans and invoices stored searchable with OCR.

items.title: Photo library (Immich)
items.desc: Our own alternative to cloud photo services with face recognition and search — all local.

items.title: Switch hardened
items.desc: Protection against cable loops and broadcast storms — without ever cutting the internet connection.

items.title: No telemetry leaving the network
items.desc: Two services sent error and usage reports to the internet — stopped; blocked connection attempts dropped to zero.

items.title: Hangs of up to a minute
items.desc: A response format the server rejected caused retry loops; internally JARVIS now uses a simple line-based format.

items.title: Slow place search
items.desc: Up to 76 seconds because a public map service was overloaded — now about 5 seconds thanks to a fallback service, caching and nightly preloading.

items.title: Outdated facts
items.desc: Names now need the same evidence as numbers; offices are looked up via the office rather than a person.

items.title: Sluggish start
items.desc: The first voice commands after start-up took up to 15 seconds; speech recognition and the language model are now pre-warmed.

items.title: Network hangs on single nodes
items.desc: Brief dropouts of a Pi’s network interface are reset within 5 seconds, and the control plane and GitOps tolerate short outages; whether the new kernel prevents them entirely is still being observed.

items.title: Language model pushed out of memory
items.desc: Cached model files filled the GPU server’s memory; limits adjusted and unused image models are unloaded.

items.title: Wrong alert count on wake-up
items.desc: When the GPU server started, two counters briefly diverged (“42 alerts”, actually one).

items.title: Empty agent answers
items.desc: Tool calls got lost because the tools were only described in text.

items.title: Missing sandbox component
items.desc: Part of the sandbox runtime had been missing since installation and was added with a verified checksum.

items.title: Wrongly counted days until Christmas
items.desc: Instead of letting the model estimate, JARVIS now calculates such questions exactly.
